steps.body:
An implicit derivative usually comes out in terms of **both x and y** — and that is not a failure. It is the honest answer.

On a circle, dy/dx = −x/y. The slope depends on WHERE you are on the curve, and a circle has two points above most x-values with opposite slopes. Only a formula mentioning y can tell them apart.
Why y has to be in the answer.
explanationVariants: Above x = 3 the circle has two points, (3, 4) and (3, −4), and their tangents have opposite slopes: −3/4 and +3/4. A formula in x alone could never give both.
dy/dx = −x/y feeds on the y-coordinate precisely so it can tell the top of the circle from the bottom.

widget.prompt: On x² + y² = 25, why does dy/dx = −x/y depend on y as well as x?

options.label: Because upper and lower points need different slopes.
options.feedback: Right. At (3, 4) the slope is −3/4 and at (3, −4) it is +3/4. A formula in x alone would have to choose one and be wrong about the other.

options.label: Because eliminating y is impossible for a circle.
options.feedback: Nothing went wrong. The dependence on y is information, not residue — it is what lets one formula serve the whole curve.

options.label: Because every implicit curve must use two variables.
options.feedback: True, and that is WHY implicit differentiation exists — but the question is what the y in the answer is doing, and it is telling the two branches apart.

options.label: Because the equation gives one point for each x.
options.feedback: You can, on the top half. Then you need a second formula for the bottom half. The implicit answer covers both at once.

steps.body: The tangent to a curve that is not a function.

widget.prompt: Build the tangent line to a circle at (3, 4).

panels.title: Differentiate the equation
panels.body: x² + y² = 25 gives 2x + 2y·(dy/dx) = 0. Every y costs a dy/dx — that is the chain rule doing its job.

panels.title: Solve for the slope
panels.body: dy/dx = −x/y. At the point (3, 4) that is −3/4. Notice we never had to write y as a function of x, and we could not have done so for the whole circle anyway.

panels.title: Then it is just a line
panels.body: A point and a slope: y − 4 = −(3/4)(x − 3). The calculus ended at the slope; the rest is the geometry you already had.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the calculus stops sooner than you expect.
widget.successFeedback: Differentiate, solve for dy/dx, substitute the point. Then it is a line through a point with a slope, and you have known how to do that for years.

steps.body: The reveal computed the slope at one point. Now hold the whole circle: slide the point and watch dy/dx come straight out of the relation — no y(x) formula ever written.

predict.prompt: A point slides to the RIGHT along the upper half of x² + y² = 25, so x grows and y shrinks. What happens to the slope dy/dx = −x/y?

options.label: Stays the same — it's one circle, one slope
Gets steeper (more negative): x is growing AND y is shrinking
Gets shallower — big circles are flat

predict.reveal: Steeper, on both counts at once: the numerator x grows while the denominator y shrinks, so −x/y falls fast. That is why the answer to an implicit derivative KEEPS y in it — the slope genuinely depends on both coordinates, which is exactly what lets you skip solving for y as a function of x.

widget.prompt: On the circle x² + y² = 25, slide the point to x = 3 and read the slope there.
widget.successFeedback: At x = 3 the circle forces y = 4, and the relation 2x + 2y·(dy/dx) = 0 hands you dy/dx = −x/y = −3/4 — the reveal's exact number, read off the point's position. You never wrote y as a function of x; the relation itself did the differentiating.
widget.explorationFeedback: Watch the readout as you slide: dy/dx = −x/y changes at every position because it depends on BOTH coordinates. That dependence is the whole reason implicit differentiation leaves y in the answer.
widget.positionFeedback: Bring the point to x = 3 — the reveal's point (3, 4) — and check the slope readout against the −3/4 the algebra produced.

explanationVariants: The tangent at (3, 4) is y − 4 = −(3/4)(x − 3). At x = 0 that gives y = 4 + 9/4 = 6.25.
The slope came from calculus; the intercept is ordinary line-work.

widget.prompt: The tangent to x² + y² = 25 at (3, 4) has slope −3/4. Find its y-intercept, as a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the y-coordinate of the POINT, not where the tangent crosses the axis. Run the line back: y = 4 + (−3/4)(0 − 3) = 4 + 2.25.
That is the circle's radius. The intercept comes from the line: 4 + 9/4 = 6.25.
Sign slip: (−3/4)(0 − 3) = +9/4, so it ADDS to 4, giving 6.25.

steps.body:
When a **product** of x and y appears, the product rule and the chain rule arrive together.

For xy: differentiate as a product — one term for each factor taking its turn — and the y-term picks up its dy/dx.

d/dx[xy] = 1·y + x·(dy/dx).
A product of the two variables.
explanationVariants: The hyperbola is falling steeply there, which is exactly what a negative slope of size 4/3 says.

widget.prompt: xy = 12. Find dy/dx at the point (3, 4), as a decimal to three places.

commonErrors.feedback: The sign is wrong. y + x·y′ = 0 gives y′ = −y/x, and on this branch the hyperbola is FALLING.
That is −x/y = −3/4 — the two variables have been swapped. Here y′ = −y/x = −4/3.
That is the constant on the right-hand side, whose derivative is 0. Differentiate the product properly: y + x·y′.

hints: Differentiate every term with respect to x. The xy term needs the PRODUCT rule; the y² term needs the CHAIN rule.
You get 2x + (y + x·y′) + 2y·y′ = 0. Now collect the y′ terms on one side.
explanationVariants: First check the point is on the curve: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 ✓. Then collect and divide — implicit differentiation is always 'differentiate, collect, divide'.

widget.prompt: x² + xy + y² = 7. Find dy/dx at (1, 2), as a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: The sign is wrong: y′(x + 2y) = −(2x + y), and the minus applies to the whole numerator.
That is the reciprocal, −5/4. The numerator is −(2x + y) = −4 and the denominator is (x + 2y) = 5.
Check the xy term: it needs the PRODUCT rule, giving y + x·y′ — two pieces, not one.

takeaways: An implicit derivative in terms of BOTH x and y is the honest answer — it is what lets one formula serve a curve with two branches.
A product of x and y needs the product rule AND the chain rule together: d/dx[xy] = y + x·y′.
The recipe never changes: differentiate every term, collect the y′ terms, divide.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: the derivatives of the whole function library — starting with the curve that is its own derivative.

concept.body: Three steps, always the same. **Differentiate** every term with respect to x, charging a y′ each time a y is differentiated. **Collect** every y′ term on one side. **Divide.** The algebra is ordinary; only the y′ bookkeeping is new.

explanationVariants: Differentiate, collect the y′, divide. Nothing else happens.

widget.prompt: x² + y² = 25. Find dy/dx at (3, 4), as a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: The sign is wrong: 2x + 2y·y′ = 0 forces y′ = −x/y, and the circle is falling at that point.
That is −y/x. On a circle the derivative is −x/y = −3/4.
